newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Eskom hopes for upgrade before next Eurobond issue.
newsitem.headline: Eskom hopes for upgrade before next Eurobond issue.

text.p: South African electricity utility Eskom is likely to wait for a hoped for upgrade in its credit rating to investment grade later this year before returning to international debt markets.

Treasury general manager Johan van den Berg told Reuters that last year's strong sales inflows and the currently high price of long term forward cover meant the parastatal was in no hurry to make an issue.
"Certainly not for the next six months we won't be looking to do it. It's really only when we start looking seriously at next year's requirement that we may, in fact, dust it off," he said.

An upgrade by Standard & Poor's for long-term foreign currency debt to an investment grade rating, from BB+ at present, could spark a quick response by Eskom, he said. S&P is expected to visit the country around September.
"If we do get an upgrade from Standard & Poor's later in the year to investment grade then one wouldn't want to wait too long to go to the market."
Van den Berg said Eskom's next Eurobond would be in German marks, despite the attractiveness of the Japanese "samurai" market in which South Africa has an established presence.

"We would still go to the German market, the reason being that it's been a while since we've been to that market and we feel sometimes we owe it to our previous investors to put some Eskom paper in the market," he said.
Eskom earlier this year put on indefinite hold plans to launch a 200 million mark five-year Eurobond because of the government's reluctance to provide forward foreign exchange cover.
Van den Berg said the central bank had since made it clear to Eskom that it would no longer offer long term forward cover.

Eskom's German Eurobond was expected to be tagged with a maturity of five to seven years and might be for more than needed to refinance its outstanding 300 million mark issue which matured in March, he said.
"We'll have to be led also by our bankers on that side. Three hundred million is not a fixed amount that we have in mind," he added.
Van den Berg said German demand for South African issues had improved from late last year when there had been oversupply of emerging market paper.
